items.stem: Which of the following best describes "semi-structured data"?
options: A field whose value uniquely identifies each record in a database table
Data about data, such as the time, location, author or device recorded with a photo or phone call
Data that has some organising tags or markers but not a rigid table structure, such as JSON or XML files
Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, text, images or sounds, that can be processed to produce information
items.answer: Data that has some organising tags or markers but not a rigid table structure, such as JSON or XML files
items.markingKey: C. "semi-structured data" is data that has some organising tags or markers but not a rigid table structure, such as JSON or XML files.

items.stem: "Qualitative data cannot be analysed by computers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Qualitative data such as text and images can be analysed using techniques like sentiment analysis, image recognition and natural language processing.
items.markingKey: Qualitative data such as text and images can be analysed using techniques like sentiment analysis, image recognition and natural language processing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Unstructured data is easier to search than structured data.
Reason (R): Structured data is organised into predefined fields and records.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. Structured data is easier to query because of its fixed format; A is false.

items.stem: With reference to sentiment analysis of tweets, explain how it illustrates turning unstructured data into structured information.
items.answer: Companies and researchers analyse millions of posts to classify them as positive, negative or neutral about brands or politicians. Natural language processing converts free text (unstructured, qualitative) into scores and categories (structured, quantitative) that can be counted and compared.
items.markingKey: Context (Companies and researchers analyse millions of posts to classify them as positive, negative or neutral about brands or politicians.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: natural language processing converts free text (unstructured, qualitative) into scores and categories (structured, quantitative) that can be counted and compared. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to turning unstructured data into structured information.

items.stem:
State whether each of the following is qualitative or quantitative data.
(a) transcripts of interviews with gig workers
(b) a table of country names and their internet-penetration rates
(c) the number of steps recorded by a fitness tracker each day
items.answer: (a) qualitative; (b) quantitative; (c) quantitative
items.markingKey: (a) qualitative; (b) quantitative; (c) quantitative. 1 mark per correct classification. Quantitative = numerical/measurable; structured = organised in a predefined format (fields, rows).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Each day the world produces quintillions of bytes of data – most of it in the form of images, video and text that fit no spreadsheet."
— Technology industry report, 2023

Explain one challenge that the type of data described in the source creates for organisations.
items.answer: Most of it is unstructured, so it cannot be easily stored in database tables or searched; organisations need specialised storage and techniques such as machine learning to extract useful information.
items.markingKey: Most of it is unstructured, so it cannot be easily stored in database tables or searched; organisations need specialised storage and techniques such as machine learning to extract useful information. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Quantitative data is more reliable than qualitative data for understanding the impact of a digital system."
items.answer: Each answers different questions; quantitative data shows scale and pattern, qualitative data explains experience and meaning, so the strongest inquiries combine both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: numbers allow comparison, scale and trends; less open to individual interpretation. Arguments against: numbers can be selected or framed to mislead; qualitative data captures experiences, meanings and causes; some impacts (dignity, trust) are hard to quantify. Supported judgement: Each answers different questions; quantitative data shows scale and pattern, qualitative data explains experience and meaning, so the strongest inquiries combine both.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that quantitative data is more reliable than qualitative data for understanding the impact of a digital system.
items.answer: Each answers different questions; quantitative data shows scale and pattern, qualitative data explains experience and meaning, so the strongest inquiries combine both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: numbers allow comparison, scale and trends; less open to individual interpretation. Arguments against: numbers can be selected or framed to mislead; qualitative data captures experiences, meanings and causes; some impacts (dignity, trust) are hard to quantify. Supported judgement: Each answers different questions; quantitative data shows scale and pattern, qualitative data explains experience and meaning, so the strongest inquiries combine both. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Briefly explain why metadata can reveal as much about a person as the content of their communications.
items.answer: Metadata shows who contacted whom, when, where and how often; patterns over time reveal relationships, routines, health concerns or political links without reading any content, which is why intelligence agencies collect it in bulk.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Metadata shows who contacted whom, when, where and how often; patterns over time reveal relationships, routines, health concerns or political links without reading any content, which is why intelligence agencies collect it in bulk. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between unstructured data and structured data.
items.answer: Structured data fits a predefined model such as database fields (easy to sort and query); unstructured data, such as images or free text, has no fixed model and needs more complex processing.
items.markingKey: Structured data fits a predefined model such as database fields (easy to sort and query); unstructured data, such as images or free text, has no fixed model and needs more complex processing. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Strava global heatmap (2018) shows how quantitative location data can reveal sensitive information.
items.answer: Strava published a heatmap of users' running and cycling routes; analysts noticed it revealed the layout of military bases where soldiers exercised with fitness trackers. Aggregated, seemingly anonymous GPS data exposed sensitive locations, showing that data types combined at scale create new meanings and risks.
items.markingKey: Context (Strava published a heatmap of users' running and cycling routes; analysts noticed it revealed the layout of military bases where soldiers exercised with fitness trackers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: aggregated, seemingly anonymous GPS data exposed sensitive locations, showing that data types combined at scale create new meanings and risks. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how quantitative location data can reveal sensitive information.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "sensor"?
options: A cookie set by a domain other than the website being visited, typically used by advertisers to track users across sites
Compression that reduces file size without losing any data, so the original can be restored exactly, such as ZIP or PNG
The number of times per second that an analogue sound wave is measured when it is digitised, measured in hertz
A device that detects a physical property such as light, temperature, motion or location and converts it into data
items.answer: A device that detects a physical property such as light, temperature, motion or location and converts it into data
items.markingKey: D. "sensor" is a device that detects a physical property such as light, temperature, motion or location and converts it into data.

items.stem: "Using private/incognito browsing makes you invisible online." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Incognito mode only stops the browser saving local history and cookies after the session; websites, internet providers and employers can still see activity, and fingerprinting still works.
items.markingKey: Incognito mode only stops the browser saving local history and cookies after the session; websites, internet providers and employers can still see activity, and fingerprinting still works. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a passive digital footprint and an active digital footprint.
items.answer: An active footprint is data you deliberately share (posts, photos); a passive footprint is data collected about you without deliberate sharing (IP address, location, cookies).
items.markingKey: An active footprint is data you deliberately share (posts, photos); a passive footprint is data collected about you without deliberate sharing (IP address, location, cookies). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"I deleted my account in 2019. In 2023 I discovered my photos were part of a facial-recognition database used by police in three countries."
— Testimony to a European data-protection authority, 2023

With reference to the source, explain why deleting an account may not remove a person's digital footprint.
items.answer: Data may already have been copied or scraped by third parties (e.g. Clearview AI) before deletion, and the person has no control over those copies.
items.markingKey: Data may already have been copied or scraped by third parties (e.g. Clearview AI) before deletion, and the person has no control over those copies. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Clearview AI shows data collection by web scraping.
items.answer: Clearview AI scraped billions of facial images from social media and websites to build a facial-recognition tool sold to police; regulators in several countries (e.g. Italy, France, the Netherlands, the UK) fined or ordered it to delete data. Images people shared for social purposes were collected without consent for a different purpose (identification), showing how public data can be repurposed.
items.markingKey: Context (Clearview AI scraped billions of facial images from social media and websites to build a facial-recognition tool sold to police; regulators in several countries (e.g. Italy, France, the Netherlands, the UK) fined or ordered it to delete data.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: images people shared for social purposes were collected without consent for a different purpose (identification), showing how public data can be repurposed. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to data collection by web scraping.

items.stem: Analyse how a smartphone collects both active and passive data during a single day of use, and evaluate how far users can control this.
items.answer: Active: messages, posts, searches, photos; passive: GPS, Wi-Fi, accelerometer, app usage, cookies, advertising ID; control: permissions, settings, Apple App Tracking Transparency (2021), limits of control (pre-installed apps, data brokers); conclude.
items.markingKey: Active: messages, posts, searches, photos; passive: GPS, Wi-Fi, accelerometer, app usage, cookies, advertising ID; control: permissions, settings, Apple App Tracking Transparency (2021), limits of control (pre-installed apps, data brokers); conclude.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "active digital footprint".
items.answer: Data a person knowingly shares, such as posts, comments, photos and form entries
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: data a person knowingly shares, such as posts, comments, photos and form entries. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A researcher sends a social-media poll about remote working to 400 people. 60 respond, and 50 of the respondents said they would prefer to work from home. (a) Calculate the response rate. (b) Calculate the percentage of respondents who would prefer to work from home.
"Sensor data from smart devices does more good than harm." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Benefits are significant where data is minimised, secured and used for clear purposes; without these safeguards, the privacy harms can outweigh them.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency in energy, transport and health monitoring; early warning (air quality, falls in elderly people). Arguments against: continuous monitoring reveals routines and habits; security weaknesses in IoT devices; data used for insurance or marketing without clear consent. Supported judgement: Benefits are significant where data is minimised, secured and used for clear purposes; without these safeguards, the privacy harms can outweigh them. Markbands (12 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Software as a Service (SaaS)"?
options: A cloud model in which applications are hosted by a provider and used over the internet, such as Google Docs or Microsoft 365
The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel in an image
Identifying a device by combining many characteristics (screen size, fonts, browser version) without storing a cookie
A group of 8 bits, which can represent 256 different values
items.answer: A cloud model in which applications are hosted by a provider and used over the internet, such as Google Docs or Microsoft 365
items.markingKey: A. "Software as a Service (SaaS)" is a cloud model in which applications are hosted by a provider and used over the internet, such as Google Docs or Microsoft 365.

items.stem: Explain why organisations increasingly store data in the cloud rather than on their own servers.
items.answer: Cloud providers offer scalable storage on demand, lower upfront costs, automatic backups and access from anywhere; organisations pay for what they use instead of buying and maintaining hardware.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Cloud providers offer scalable storage on demand, lower upfront costs, automatic backups and access from anywhere; organisations pay for what they use instead of buying and maintaining hardware. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between cloud storage and local storage.
items.answer: Local storage keeps data on devices the user owns (hard drive, USB); cloud storage keeps data on a provider's remote servers accessed over the internet, trading control for convenience and scalability.
items.markingKey: Local storage keeps data on devices the user owns (hard drive, USB); cloud storage keeps data on a provider's remote servers accessed over the internet, trading control for convenience and scalability. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A database table stores 120,000 records. Each record has the fields student ID (6 bytes), surname (30 bytes), grade (2 bytes), house (12 bytes). Calculate the size of the table in megabytes (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes), ignoring overheads.
items.answer: 6 MB

items.stem: Briefly describe Aadhaar's Central Identities Data Repository and explain what it reveals about centralised data storage and security.
items.answer: India stores Aadhaar biometric and demographic data in a central database managed by UIDAI. Centralising data on over a billion people makes services efficient but creates a high-value target, so security failures could have national consequences.
items.markingKey: Context (India stores Aadhaar biometric and demographic data in a central database managed by UIDAI.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: centralising data on over a billion people makes services efficient but creates a high-value target, so security failures could have national consequences. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to centralised data storage and security.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"There is no cloud, it's just someone else's computer."
— Popular slogan printed on stickers and T-shirts in the tech community, c. 2014

Explain what the source suggests about cloud storage.
items.answer: Cloud data is stored on physical servers owned and controlled by another organisation, so users depend on that provider for security, availability and privacy.
items.markingKey: Cloud data is stored on physical servers owned and controlled by another organisation, so users depend on that provider for security, availability and privacy. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Explain why the location of data centres matters for digital society.
items.answer: Data centres use large amounts of electricity and water, so their location affects local energy grids and environments; they are also subject to the laws of the country where they are, which affects privacy and government access.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Data centres use large amounts of electricity and water, so their location affects local energy grids and environments; they are also subject to the laws of the country where they are, which affects privacy and government access. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ana writes: "Data in the cloud cannot be lost." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Cloud data can be lost through outages, accidental deletion, ransomware, account closure or provider failure (e.g. the 2021 OVHcloud data-centre fire in Strasbourg destroyed customer data).
items.markingKey: Cloud data can be lost through outages, accidental deletion, ransomware, account closure or provider failure (e.g. the 2021 OVHcloud data-centre fire in Strasbourg destroyed customer data). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "bit"?
options: A group of 8 bits, which can represent 256 different values
A cookie set by a domain other than the website being visited, typically used by advertisers to track users across sites
A single binary digit, 0 or 1 – the smallest unit of data
Data about data, such as the time, location, author or device recorded with a photo or phone call
items.answer: A single binary digit, 0 or 1 – the smallest unit of data
items.markingKey: C. "bit" is a single binary digit, 0 or 1 – the smallest unit of data.

items.stem: Briefly explain why computers use binary to represent data.
items.answer: Digital electronics have two stable states (on/off, high/low voltage) that are reliable to store and distinguish, so all data – numbers, text, images and sound – is encoded as patterns of 0s and 1s.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Digital electronics have two stable states (on/off, high/low voltage) that are reliable to store and distinguish, so all data – numbers, text, images and sound – is encoded as patterns of 0s and 1s. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
A row of pixels in a black-and-white image is stored as: WWWWWWWBBBBBWWWWWWW
Using run-length encoding (RLE), write the encoded form (e.g. 3W2B) and state how many characters are saved.
items.answer: 7W5B7W; saves 13 characters (19 → 6)
items.markingKey: Runs: 7 × W, 5 × B, 7 × W → 7W5B7W [A1 A1]; 19 − 6 = 13 characters saved [A1]. RLE is lossless.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Emoji are now part of Unicode, which means the same smiley sent from Lagos appears – more or less – the same in Lima."
— Article on digital communication, 2022

Explain why a shared encoding standard matters for communication.
items.answer: A shared standard maps each character/emoji to the same code, so different devices and platforms interpret it consistently; without it, text would appear garbled across systems (though fonts may draw emoji differently).
items.markingKey: A shared standard maps each character/emoji to the same code, so different devices and platforms interpret it consistently; without it, text would appear garbled across systems (though fonts may draw emoji differently). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Understanding binary is irrelevant for understanding digital society."
items.answer: Detailed binary arithmetic is not the focus, but understanding representation helps explain real impacts such as access, inclusion and privacy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most impacts can be analysed without technical detail; users interact with interfaces, not bits. Arguments against: representation explains file sizes, compression and bandwidth inequality; encoding choices affect languages included online; metadata and data formats shape privacy. Supported judgement: Detailed binary arithmetic is not the focus, but understanding representation helps explain real impacts such as access, inclusion and privacy.

items.stem: Briefly explain why lossy compression is commonly used for streaming video and music.
items.answer: It greatly reduces file size by removing detail people barely notice, so content can be streamed over limited bandwidth and stored cheaply, at the cost of some quality.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It greatly reduces file size by removing detail people barely notice, so content can be streamed over limited bandwidth and stored cheaply, at the cost of some quality. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A charity in a rural area with slow internet wants to share training videos with volunteers. Explain how data representation and compression could help, and evaluate one trade-off.
items.answer: Reduce resolution/frame rate, use lossy codecs (H.264), audio at lower sample rate, offer downloadable versions; trade-off: smaller files vs lower quality/readability of on-screen text; mention calculation of file size and bandwidth.
items.markingKey: Reduce resolution/frame rate, use lossy codecs (H.264), audio at lower sample rate, offer downloadable versions; trade-off: smaller files vs lower quality/readability of on-screen text; mention calculation of file size and bandwidth.

items.stem: In 2012, a photo posted online revealed the location of fugitive John McAfee in Guatemala. What revealed it?
options: Facial recognition
A hacked email
His IP address in a tweet
GPS metadata in the photo's EXIF data
items.answer: GPS metadata in the photo's EXIF data
items.markingKey: D. Vice published a photo whose EXIF data included GPS coordinates.

items.stem: Which sensor in a smartphone detects the orientation and movement of the phone?
options: Ambient light sensor
Microphone
Accelerometer/gyroscope
Proximity sensor only
items.answer: Accelerometer/gyroscope
items.markingKey: C. Accelerometers and gyroscopes measure motion and rotation, used in step counting.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A database that stores data in linked tables of rows (records) and columns (fields), queried with languages such as SQL"?
options: qualitative data
relational database
cloud storage
database
items.answer: relational database
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of relational database.

items.stem: Explain the difference between lossless compression and lossy compression.
items.answer: Lossy compression permanently removes some data to make files much smaller (JPEG, MP3); lossless compression shrinks files without losing data, so the original can be exactly restored (ZIP, PNG, FLAC).
items.markingKey: Lossy compression permanently removes some data to make files much smaller (JPEG, MP3); lossless compression shrinks files without losing data, so the original can be exactly restored (ZIP, PNG, FLAC). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A photo shared online can reveal where it was taken even if the image shows no landmarks.
Reason (R): Many cameras and phones store GPS coordinates in the image's EXIF metadata.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Location metadata travels with the file unless removed.

items.stem: Briefly explain why passive data collection raises greater privacy concerns than active data collection.
items.answer: Users often do not know passive data is being collected (location, browsing, device identifiers), so they cannot give meaningful consent or control it, and it can be combined to build detailed profiles.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Users often do not know passive data is being collected (location, browsing, device identifiers), so they cannot give meaningful consent or control it, and it can be combined to build detailed profiles. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A database is just a big spreadsheet." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Databases enforce structure (data types, primary keys), link tables through relationships, support many simultaneous users and are queried with languages such as SQL, unlike a single spreadsheet.
items.markingKey: Databases enforce structure (data types, primary keys), link tables through relationships, support many simultaneous users and are queried with languages such as SQL, unlike a single spreadsheet. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Increasing the colour depth of an image does not change its file size." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: More bits per pixel means more data per pixel, so the file size increases proportionally (size = width × height × colour depth).
items.markingKey: More bits per pixel means more data per pixel, so the file size increases proportionally (size = width × height × colour depth). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between quantitative data and qualitative data.
items.answer: Qualitative data describes qualities in words or images (e.g. interview responses); quantitative data is numerical and measurable (e.g. download speed in Mbps).
items.markingKey: Qualitative data describes qualities in words or images (e.g. interview responses); quantitative data is numerical and measurable (e.g. download speed in Mbps). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An air-quality sensor at a school in Hanoi logs one measurement every 60 seconds. Calculate how many measurements are recorded in 1 hour.
items.answer: 60 measurements

items.stem:
A school database table Students contains:
Name | City | Age | Level
Amara | Nairobi | 17 | HL
Mei | Hanoi | 18 | HL
Kenji | Seoul | 18 | SL
Lukas | Vienna | 16 | SL
Diego | Bogotá | 16 | SL
Sofia | Lima | 16 | HL

State the names returned by the query: SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Level = 'HL'; Then identify the field that would be most suitable as a primary key if a StudentID field were not available, and explain why Name is a poor choice.
items.answer: Amara, Mei, Sofia; no existing field is guaranteed unique – Name can be repeated, so a unique StudentID should be added
items.markingKey: Amara, Mei, Sofia [A1 for all correct, A1 for no extras]. Primary key must be unique for every record; names (and cities, ages) can repeat, so none is suitable – a unique ID is needed [R1 R1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which the spread of MP3 and file sharing shows how data representation shapes social change.
items.answer: The MP3 format (developed at the Fraunhofer Institute in the early 1990s) shrank music files by about 90%; Napster (1999) let millions share them, disrupting the recorded-music industry. Lossy compression made music small enough to share over slow internet connections, enabling peer-to-peer sharing and, later, streaming business models.
items.markingKey: Context (The MP3 format (developed at the Fraunhofer Institute in the early 1990s) shrank music files by about 90%; Napster (1999) let millions share them, disrupting the recorded-music industry.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: lossy compression made music small enough to share over slow internet connections, enabling peer-to-peer sharing and, later, streaming business models. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how data representation shapes social change.

items.stem: "Metadata is harmless because it does not include the content of a message." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Metadata (who, when, where, how long) can reveal relationships, movements and habits; former NSA director Michael Hayden said "we kill people based on metadata".
items.markingKey: Metadata (who, when, where, how long) can reveal relationships, movements and habits; former NSA director Michael Hayden said "we kill people based on metadata". 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"By clicking Accept All, you agree to the use of cookies by us and our 847 partners."
— Cookie consent banner on a news website, 2024

Explain one problem with this form of consent.
items.answer: Users cannot realistically read or understand the policies of 847 partners, so "consent" is not genuinely informed; banners often nudge users to accept (dark patterns).
items.markingKey: Users cannot realistically read or understand the policies of 847 partners, so "consent" is not genuinely informed; banners often nudge users to accept (dark patterns). Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Leila has 2,500 photos on a phone, each about 6 MB. Calculate the total storage in GB (1 GB = 1000 MB). A cloud plan offers 15 GB. State whether the photos fit and how much space remains or is lacking.
items.answer: 15 GB; fits, 0 GB remain

items.stem: A sound clip is recorded at a sample rate of 44,100 Hz with a bit depth of 8 bits, in stereo, for 30 seconds. Calculate the uncompressed file size in megabytes (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes).

A city installs smart bins that record fill level, collection times and photos of dumped rubbish. Classify the data collected and evaluate one benefit and one risk of combining it with residents' metadata.
items.answer: Fill level and times: quantitative, structured; photos: qualitative, unstructured; metadata: location/time stamps. Benefit: efficient collection routes and less fuel. Risk: photos and location/time data could identify individuals, raising privacy and surveillance concerns. Reward correct classification and balanced evaluation.
items.markingKey: Fill level and times: quantitative, structured; photos: qualitative, unstructured; metadata: location/time stamps. Benefit: efficient collection routes and less fuel. Risk: photos and location/time data could identify individuals, raising privacy and surveillance concerns. Reward correct classification and balanced evaluation.

items.stem: "Users are responsible for the size of their own digital footprint." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Users control part of their active footprint, but passive collection by platforms and data brokers means responsibility lies largely with organisations and regulators.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: users choose what to post and which apps to use; privacy settings and ad blockers are available. Arguments against: much data is collected passively and invisibly; consent banners are designed to nudge acceptance; others can post data about you. Supported judgement: Users control part of their active footprint, but passive collection by platforms and data brokers means responsibility lies largely with organisations and regulators. items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that storing personal data in the cloud is safer than storing it on personal devices.
items.answer: For most users the cloud is safer against loss and many attacks, but it shifts risks to provider security and legal access; strong passwords, 2FA and encryption matter.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: professional security, encryption and redundancy; automatic backups protect against device loss. Arguments against: large providers are attractive targets for hackers; users lose control and depend on provider policies; governments may access data under local laws. Supported judgement: For most users the cloud is safer against loss and many attacks, but it shifts risks to provider security and legal access; strong passwords, 2FA and encryption matter. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the benefits of lossy compression outweigh its drawbacks.
items.answer: For everyday media consumption benefits clearly outweigh drawbacks, but lossless formats remain essential where accuracy matters.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: enables streaming and video calls on limited bandwidth; reduces storage costs and energy. Arguments against: permanent quality loss, problematic for archives, medical images and evidence; repeated compression degrades quality. items.stem: Define the term "metadata".
items.answer: Data about data, such as the time, location, author or device recorded with a photo or phone call
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: data about data, such as the time, location, author or device recorded with a photo or phone call. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The trail of data a person leaves through online activity, both actively (posts) and passively (browsing, location)"?
options: third-party cookie
digital footprint
quantitative data
unstructured data
items.answer: digital footprint
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of digital footprint.

items.stem: Which of the following is a cloud service model in which the provider supplies virtual servers and storage that customers manage themselves?
options: Software as a Service (SaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Peer-to-peer networking
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
items.answer: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
items.markingKey: D. IaaS (e.g. Amazon EC2) provides computing infrastructure; customers install and manage their own software.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Increasing the colour depth of an image does not change its file size." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: More bits per pixel means more data per pixel, so the file size increases proportionally (size = width × height × colour depth).
items.markingKey: More bits per pixel means more data per pixel, so the file size increases proportionally (size = width × height × colour depth). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why most of the data created today is unstructured.
items.answer: Much data comes from photos, videos, voice messages, emails and social-media posts, which do not fit into predefined fields; this makes it harder to search and analyse without techniques such as machine learning.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Much data comes from photos, videos, voice messages, emails and social-media posts, which do not fit into predefined fields; this makes it harder to search and analyse without techniques such as machine learning. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between browser fingerprinting and a cookie.
items.answer: A cookie is a file stored on the user's browser that the user can delete; fingerprinting identifies a device from its characteristics without storing anything, so it is harder to block.
items.markingKey: A cookie is a file stored on the user's browser that the user can delete; fingerprinting identifies a device from its characteristics without storing anything, so it is harder to block. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between local storage and cloud storage.
items.answer: Local storage keeps data on devices the user owns (hard drive, USB); cloud storage keeps data on a provider's remote servers accessed over the internet, trading control for convenience and scalability.
items.markingKey: Local storage keeps data on devices the user owns (hard drive, USB); cloud storage keeps data on a provider's remote servers accessed over the internet, trading control for convenience and scalability. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between lossy compression and lossless compression.
items.answer: Lossy compression permanently removes some data to make files much smaller (JPEG, MP3); lossless compression shrinks files without losing data, so the original can be exactly restored (ZIP, PNG, FLAC).
items.markingKey: Lossy compression permanently removes some data to make files much smaller (JPEG, MP3); lossless compression shrinks files without losing data, so the original can be exactly restored (ZIP, PNG, FLAC). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Qualitative data cannot be analysed by computers." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Qualitative data such as text and images can be analysed using techniques like sentiment analysis, image recognition and natural language processing.
items.markingKey: Qualitative data such as text and images can be analysed using techniques like sentiment analysis, image recognition and natural language processing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A researcher sends an email survey about online banking to 400 people. 60 respond, and 49 of the respondents said they prefer banking through an app. (a) Calculate the response rate. (b) Calculate the percentage of respondents who prefer banking through an app.
Using the OVHcloud fire in Strasbourg (2021) as an example, explain the physical reality of cloud storage.
items.answer: In March 2021 a fire destroyed one of OVHcloud's data-centre buildings in Strasbourg, taking millions of websites offline; some customers without off-site backups permanently lost data. The "cloud" is physical infrastructure that can fail, so backup strategies and redundancy across locations are essential.
items.markingKey: Context (In March 2021 a fire destroyed one of OVHcloud's data-centre buildings in Strasbourg, taking millions of websites offline; some customers without off-site backups permanently lost data.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the "cloud" is physical infrastructure that can fail, so backup strategies and redundancy across locations are essential. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the physical reality of cloud storage.

Classify each of the following as qualitative or quantitative, and as structured or unstructured.
(a) the price and quantity of each item in a supermarket sales database
(b) the colour of cars recorded in a car-park database as a category field
(c) the number of steps recorded by a fitness tracker each day
items.answer: (a) quantitative, structured; (b) qualitative, structured; (c) quantitative, structured
items.markingKey: (a) quantitative, structured; (b) qualitative, structured; (c) quantitative, structured. 1 mark per correct classification. Quantitative = numerical/measurable; structured = organised in a predefined format (fields, rows).

items.stem: "Deleting your social-media posts removes your digital footprint." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Passive data, copies, screenshots, backups and data held by third parties (advertisers, data brokers) remain; deletion only removes part of the active footprint.
items.markingKey: Passive data, copies, screenshots, backups and data held by third parties (advertisers, data brokers) remain; deletion only removes part of the active footprint. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A school database table Students contains:
Name | City | Age | Level
Lukas | Vienna | 16 | SL
Priya | Mumbai | 17 | HL
Amara | Nairobi | 17 | HL
Sofia | Lima | 16 | HL
Kenji | Seoul | 18 | SL
Mei | Hanoi | 18 | HL

State the names returned by the query: SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Age > 16; Then identify the field that would be most suitable as a primary key if a StudentID field were not available, and explain why Name is a poor choice.
items.answer: Priya, Amara, Kenji, Mei; no existing field is guaranteed unique – Name can be repeated, so a unique StudentID should be added
items.markingKey: Priya, Amara, Kenji, Mei [A1 for all correct, A1 for no extras]. Primary key must be unique for every record; names (and cities, ages) can repeat, so none is suitable – a unique ID is needed [R1 R1].

items.stem: Convert the denary number 205 into hexadecimal, showing your working.
items.answer: CD
items.markingKey: 205 ÷ 16 = 12 remainder 13 → CD (binary 11001101) [M1 A1].

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Metadata should be protected by law as strongly as the content of communications."
items.answer: Because aggregated metadata can be as revealing as content, it deserves strong protection, with narrowly defined exceptions overseen by courts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: metadata reveals relationships, health and political links; it is collected in bulk without users' awareness. Arguments against: security agencies argue metadata is essential and less intrusive than reading content; some metadata is needed to run networks. Supported judgement: Because aggregated metadata can be as revealing as content, it deserves strong protection, with narrowly defined exceptions overseen by courts.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that users are responsible for the size of their own digital footprint.
items.answer: Users control part of their active footprint, but passive collection by platforms and data brokers means responsibility lies largely with organisations and regulators.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: users choose what to post and which apps to use; privacy settings and ad blockers are available. Arguments against: much data is collected passively and invisibly; consent banners are designed to nudge acceptance; others can post data about you. Supported judgement: Users control part of their active footprint, but passive collection by platforms and data brokers means responsibility lies largely with organisations and regulators. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: A hospital is deciding whether to move patient records from its own servers to a cloud provider. Evaluate this decision for two stakeholders.
items.answer: Stakeholders: patients (privacy, availability), hospital (cost, scalability, security responsibility), staff (access), regulators (GDPR/HIPAA compliance, data location); consider breaches, outages, vendor lock-in; reach a recommendation.
items.markingKey: Stakeholders: patients (privacy, availability), hospital (cost, scalability, security responsibility), staff (access), regulators (GDPR/HIPAA compliance, data location); consider breaches, outages, vendor lock-in; reach a recommendation.
